title: Salary Raise Calculator: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Salary Raise Calculator: Your new salary after a raise — yearly, monthly and hourly. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and answers…
content:
The [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Your new salary after a raise — yearly, monthly and hourly. Enter your current annual salary, raise and hours per week and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Work out your new salary after a raise: enter your current pay and the raise as a percentage, and see the new annual salary plus the increase broken down by year, month and hour. A 5% raise on $65,000 is $3,250 a year — $271 a month before tax. Remember the figures are gross: tax, retirement contributions and other deductions come out of the new salary too, so the take-home increase is smaller. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Salary Raise Calculator

Start by entering your current annual salary ($), then entering your raise (%) and finally entering your hours per week. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter your current annual salary and the raise percentage.
2. Adjust the hours per week if you work something other than 40.
3. Read your new salary, and the increase per year, month and hour.

## Formula

Increase = current salary × raise %. New salary = current salary + increase. Monthly = annual ÷ 12. Hourly = annual ÷ (hours per week × 52).

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 5% raise on a $65,000 salary adds $3,250 a year, taking the salary to $68,250 — $5,687.50 a month and $32.81 an hour at 40 hours a week. Try the same figures in the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Current annual salary: 65000 $, Raise: 5 %, Hours per week: 40), the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) returns New annual salary: $68,250, Increase per year: $3,250, Increase per month: $270.83, New monthly pay: $5,687.5, New hourly rate: $32.81. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Percentage vs. amount

Raises are usually quoted as percentages, which makes them easy to compare — but a percentage of a small salary is a small amount. A 5% raise on $40,000 is $2,000; the same 5% on $120,000 is $6,000. When comparing offers, look at the amount and the new total, not just the percentage.

## The raise is gross, not take-home

The increase shown here is before tax. A $3,250 raise does not add $3,250 to your bank account: federal and state tax, Social Security and Medicare all take a share, and a higher salary can push part of your pay into a higher bracket. Use the paycheck calculator to see what the raise is worth after tax.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Compare offers by the new total, not just the percentage.
- Check the after-tax value with the paycheck calculator.
- A raise also lifts anything tied to salary, like 401(k) matches.

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I calculate a salary raise?

Multiply your current salary by the raise percentage, then add it on. A 5% raise on $65,000 is $65,000 × 0.05 = $3,250, so the new salary is $68,250. Try it with your own numbers in the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is a good raise percentage?

It varies by industry and year, but 3–5% a year is typical for a standard performance raise, and more for a promotion or a move to a new role. Anything below inflation is a pay cut in real terms. Try it with your own numbers in the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Is the raise amount before or after tax?

Before tax. Tax, Social Security, Medicare and retirement contributions all come out of the new salary, so the take-home increase is smaller. Try it with your own numbers in the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How do I work out my new hourly rate?

Divide the new annual salary by hours per week × 52. At 40 hours a week, $68,250 a year is $68,250 ÷ 2,080 = $32.81 an hour. Try it with your own numbers in the [Salary Raise Calculator](/salary-raise-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
